1uouK7mzsxuY1Xx9F4_ZjfG_Bv5--HSbX.indexNote: Hampi, the city of ruins. In early 2019, I explored its ancient grandeur with a new mirrorless camera, drawn to black and white. Every stone held a story; beside the Tungabhadra, Virupaksha Temple felt timeless.
1uouK7mzsxuY1Xx9F4_ZjfG_Bv5--HSbX.note: Hampi, the city of ruins, where every stone seems to hold a story. I visited in early 2019 with a newly bought mirrorless camera, and its ancient character felt perfect for experimenting with black and white. The monochrome frames brought out a sense of longing, age, and the forgotten grandeur of the Vijayanagara Empire. Seeing the ruins today, I could only imagine how magnificent this city must have been in its full glory. And by the banks of the Tungabhadra, the Virupaksha Temple still stands: timeless, silent, and unforgettable.

experience.title: My first forest
paragraphs: I was seven when I first visited Kanha National Park in 2004. It was early March, spring in North India, and the evening air was turning chilly. Film cameras were what we had access to then. I did not know that one evening in the forest would stay with me for so long.

I still remember the gypsies parked beside a dried-up lake bed. On one side of the road, the ground sloped down towards the lake bed; on the other, tall grass stretched across the meadow. Someone in one of the gypsies had spotted a tiger in the bushes. Our driver was sure it might cross the road and go down towards the lake bed, so we waited with everyone else.

We stayed there for around half an hour. The sun was setting at the edge of my vision when a naturalist in the first jeep noticed movement in the bushes along the meadow. Within five minutes, the tiger appeared: a young male, perhaps three or four years old. The naturalist told us he had recently separated from his mother.

He came within about ten feet of me. Around fifteen jeeps had gathered, with people taking pictures and gasping at the sight. In all that chaos, I had only one real glance. But I remember the almost royal confidence in the way he moved. He crossed the road without hesitation, as though none of us were there.
That was the moment I fell in love with wildlife. The thrill of seeing a tiger so close was immense, and so was the respect I felt for the animal and its natural habitat.

After the trip, we waited for the film to be developed at the shop. When the photographs came back, I could hardly believe what my dad had captured: the tiger leaping from the gravel into the lake bed. He had made that picture with a film camera, with no display to check and no second take. It happened in an instant, and he caught it. Seeing those photographs made me want to find moments like that through my own camera.

My fondness for wildlife and my respect for the places it lives have only grown since that day. This collection is a small personal tribute to the 17 national parks I have visited over the years, and to the journey that began in Kanha.
